extracted.intended_audience: USPTO staff, patent practitioners, and biotechnology/pharmaceutical stakeholders
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether a patent specification enables the full scope of claimed subject matter (with emphasis on broad genus claims such as antibody genera). Summarizes Supreme Court holdings, precedent, and practical factors courts use in enablement/written-description disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement requirement — enable full scope of the claims
rubrics_metrics.description: "If a patent claims an entire class of processes, machines, manufactures, or compositions of matter, the patent’s specification must enable a person skilled in the art to make and use the entire class. In other words, the specification must enable the full scope of the invention as defined by its claims." (Amgen, 143 S.Ct. at 1254)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key principle: the specification must enable the full scope of claimed subject matter. Practical implication: when a claim seeks broad coverage (a genus), the specification must provide enabling disclosure across that claimed breadth. Courts will evaluate whether the specification enables "all of what is claimed, not merely a subset."

rubrics_metrics.name: Amount of disclosure — examples plus a disclosed general quality can suffice
rubrics_metrics.description: "The specification does not always need to 'describe with particularity how to make and use every single embodiment within a claimed class.' ... For instance, it may suffice to give an example (or a few examples) if the specification also discloses some general quality . . . running through the class that gives it a peculiar fitness for the particular purpose." (Amgen, 143 S.Ct. at 1254-55)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance for sufficiency: specific examples can be adequate when paired with disclosure of a general, class-wide quality that reliably enables skilled artisans to make and use the full class. Evaluate whether the disclosed examples + general trait reasonably allow practice across the claimed genus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimentation must be reasonable
rubrics_metrics.description: "The specification may call for a reasonable amount of experimentation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permissible amount of follow-on work is limited to "reasonable" experimentation. Courts assess whether the experimentation required to practice the claim is reasonable given the nature of the invention and the underlying art; excessive or undue experimentation indicates lack of enablement.

rubrics_metrics.name: The more claimed, the more must be enabled (claim breadth vs disclosure)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The more one claims, the more one must enable." (Amgen, 143 S.Ct. at 1254)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule of thumb: broader claim scope demands proportionally greater enabling disclosure. Narrow claims covering specific embodiments require less expansive disclosure than claims that assert an entire class or "kingdom" of subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wands factors are probative in enablement inquiries
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the Supreme Court did not cite Wands, "the Wands factors appear at least probative of the essential inquiry in determining whether one must engage in reasonable experimentation."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Wands factors (level of ordinary skill, predictability of the art, amount of guidance in the disclosure, presence of working examples, breadth of the claims, nature of the invention, and the quantity of experimentation necessary) as an evidentiary framework to assess enablement's reasonableness and scope. Courts (including CAFC) have applied Wands in evaluating enablement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written-description requirement (distinct but related)
rubrics_metrics.description: Litigation history shows written description was separately evaluated (juries and courts assessed whether claims were adequately described).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat written description as a separate statutory requirement from enablement. A specification must demonstrate that the inventor possessed the claimed invention (written description) as well as teach how to make and use it (enablement). Procedural note: jury instructions and evidentiary rulings on written description can be pivotal in litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precedent/analogy to prior cases (Morse, Incandescent Lamp, Holland Furniture, Wood & Mineral Separation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court analyzed Amgen in light of prior decisions: Morse, Incandescent Lamp, Holland Furniture, and Wood & Mineral Separation; these cases teach that claiming excessively broad subject matter without commensurate enablement fails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogize to historical precedents that struck down claims attempting 'sovereignty over [an] entire kingdom' of subject matter. Consider lessons from older cases (e.g., that a specification may tolerate some experimentation but reasonableness depends on the invention and prior art).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent bargain (policy backdrop)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent bargain: Quid pro quo — Inventor discloses the invention; Inventor receives a limited term of protection. Congress has left the enablement requirement intact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy reminder: enablement is rooted in the patent bargain — disclosure must be sufficient to justify the granted exclusion. This policy frame informs strictness of enablement analysis, especially for broad claims.
